lignes.texte: Headlines scream about China owning America’s debt.
Except… they walked away years ago. Right now, Western superpowers are
spending more cash just paying interest than on their entire defense budgets. Trillions of
unbuyable bonds are flooding the markets, causing the financial system to grind to a halt, forcing a
shadowy private buyer to step into the vacuum. The global economy is on life support.
And it only takes one single margin call to pull the plug.
In late August, 2026, the United States Treasury sold
$25 billion in 30 year bonds at a 5.216% yield. That’s the highest borrowing rate since 2001.
And that’s important. Because when US Treasury
bonds rates spike like this, the shockwaves rip through the entire global economy.
That’s how influential American bonds are. They dictate everything from corporate credit
rates to monthly mortgage payments, at home and abroad. The government successfully dumped its
debt this time around, but who is buying bonds from a country drowning in $40 trillion of debt?
The U.S. hit that astronomical tally in August 2026. It took over 2 centuries, including 2
world wars, to hit a trillion of national debt. By January 2017, that number had soared to almost $20
trillion. That figure has more than doubled less than a decade later. These days, the US government
effectively adds another trillion dollars to its balance sheet every 5 months, on average.
It’s an eyewatering sum. But the “debt to GDP
ratio” is even more concerning. That number compares a country’s
total national debt to its gross domestic product (GDP). It basically shows how capable a country
is of paying back the money it owes. America’s debt exceeds 124% of its GDP.
It’s one of the worst ratios on Earth. Only a few select countries rank lower,
including Japan, Sudan, Venezuela, and Greece. And it only gets worse from there. The annual
interest payments alone on America’s debt have now crossed the $1 trillion mark.
The US would have to spend more than its entire national defense budget every single year just to
cover the interest costs on the debt it owes. And that’s without making a dent in the debt itself.
Of course, America isn’t the only country in this sort of situation.
A Bloomberg report revealed that most of the G7 nations are spending more on debt interest than
defense. The numbers are staggering. Italy spends 193% of its defense budget on debt interest, for
example. The UK pays 105%, and France hits 103%. But the U.S. is in a more dangerous position.
No other nation comes close to the US when it comes to the absolute enormity of the country’s
overall debt. For decades, the global financial system operated according to an unwritten but
all-important rule: US debt was the safest place to store capital. Whenever Washington DC decided
to issue some fresh debt, the same familiar faces were happy to snap it up in large amounts.
First in line were the Central Banks from countries like China, Japan, Western European
powerhouses, and the Gulf States. Buying US bonds was an obvious move that made absolute
economic sense, both in the short term and from a big picture perspective. It also helped them
keep the values of their own currencies under control against the dollar. It also helped keep
export and import prices sustainable. Bonds provided instant liquidity,
since they could be sold, traded, and cashed in at any time. But the longer central banks were
able to hold onto them, the more value they could feasibly make from their investments. So, these
countries had no problem swallowing up hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of Treasuries.
But foreign powers weren’t the only ones soaking up America’s debt.
The Federal Reserve also weaponized the system. They bought up billions of Treasuries to influence
interest rates and prop up the economy. Whatever debt was left was hoovered up by pension funds
and insurance giants. They all provided the stable foundation for American debt.
It helped to increase the price of bonds while lowering their yields. That made it easier
for the US government to finance its budget and spend on defense, infrastructure and education.
But now, that foundation is cracking. The American economy is beginning to crumble.
The foreign Central Banks haven’t bailed out entirely, but they’re heading towards… at speed.
While Japan is still America’s largest foreign creditor, with over a trillion dollars’ worth
of Treasuries. The UK holds another $900 billion in bonds. But other major players
are getting out while they can. Chief among them is China.
It used to be the second biggest holder of American debt and peaked at around $1.3 trillion.
Today, it holds about half of that: $633 billion, to be exact.
And it’s not a one-off. It’s just one part of a larger trend.
Central Banks around the world have been slashing their holdings of US debt over the
last couple of decades. Around the time of the 2008 financial crisis, foreign governments held
around 40% of American debt. These days, it’s 12%.
These countries didn’t just ease up a little on their investments;
they dropped off dramatically. They weren’t the only ones. The pension funds started pulling out,
too. For years, they’d been so reliable. In order to provide the guaranteed monthly
payouts they promised to retirees, these funds had no other choice but to buy 30-year Treasury
bonds. They could always be counted on to take their share of America’s debt.
But there’s been a shift in corporate America. People are turning their backs on defined-benefit
pensions and towards systems, like 401(k)s. And with 401(k)s proving more popular and appealing,
pension funds no longer need to tie up their investments in low-yield 30-year Treasuries.
They can focus on making the most money out of private equity and high-yield credit, instead.
The timing couldn’t be worse. The US government is setting
new records for national debt. Its interest payments are spiraling out of control. And
it needs buyers who are willing to buy-in to bonds for an extended period of time.
Now those buyers are vanishing. Every year the Treasury needs to
offload $2 trillion of fresh debt it accumulates each year. It also has to refinance the trillions
of pre-existing debt as it approaches its expiry date. When demand drops, the Treasury has one move
left: to jack up interest rates to attract buyers. In August 2026, long-term Treasury yields reached
highs that hadn’t been seen in over 20 years. Tens of millions of American homeowners suddenly
faced the very real threat of sudden mortgage rate spikes to match. The Treasury Secretary,
Scott Bessent, had to step in and take drastic action to control the situation.
To calm the panicking markets, Bessent announced that Washington would double its bond buybacks.
To foot the bill, Washington is flooding the market with short term Treasury bills that
mature in months, not years. It was a desperate move.
It was like paying off a credit card with a handful of smaller cards.
While it provided some short-term relief, it came at a massive cost. Washington admitted to the
world that the sovereign bond market was broken. The government was having to artificially
manipulate the system just to keep the lights on. So if pension funds and foreign Central Banks
aren’t buying up US debt anymore, who is? A collective of hyper-leveraged, private,
macro hedge funds. And they’re following
an extremely dangerous trading strategy. To stop another financial meltdown like the
2008 crisis, financial regulators issued a new rulebook called Basel III. Under these rules,
giants like the Bank of America and JP Morgan were told they had to have vast cash reserves available
at all times. They couldn’t take huge risks and leverage their capital like they had before.
It brought some kind of stability to the banking sector. But it also had a vicious
knock-on effect on the global financial system. Before the rule change, big banks acted like
the shock absorbers for American debt. When the Treasury auctioned off billions in bonds,
the banks swallowed the supply into their own balance sheets. Then they distributed the funds
to investors around the world. The new rules changed that.
The shock absorbers were gone. Again, the timing couldn’t have been
worse. Right as US debt was exploding, banks were being handcuffed. It’s not profitable
for banks to hold such huge amounts of debt, so other entities had to step in and fill the void.
The hedge funds. They don’t need to worry
about Basel III or other regulations. They don’t need to concern themselves with leverage limits or
arbitrary authorities. They have more freedom to put their money wherever they want it… as
long as it provides a reasonable return. That’s the big difference between these
funds – the new owners of American debt – and the central banks and pension funds that came before
them. They’re not in this for the long haul. They’re in it for profit.
That means they’re happy to cash out within months, weeks, days,
or even hours after buying in. As long as they’re in a better position, that’s all that matters. To
make sure they end up winning, they rely on a financial mechanism known as the cash-futures
basis trade, or basis trade, for short. On paper, a physical U.S. bond and a bond
futures contract should cost the same amount. But they don’t. The futures contracts are
often a micro-fraction more expensive. For you, the difference is worthless. But for
hedge funds gambling on billions of dollars, that micro-fraction of a penny adds up to huge profits.
That’s where the basis trade comes in. If a hedge fund sees that a physical
30-year bond is trading at a tiny discount compared to a 30-year futures contract,
they buy the physical bond. Meanwhile, they short, or sell, the corresponding contract.
They lock in both sides, creating a risk free profit.
But to make it really lucrative, they use a loophole called the “Repo” market.
The hedge fund takes the freshly purchased bond straight to a bank,
which accepts it as collateral. Then, the bank hands over cash at near zero interest.
But instead of pocketing it, the hedge fund buys another bond, shorts another contract
and uses the new bond to borrow more money. They do this over and over again. They borrow
more and more cash to supercharge their investment and profits. By recycling the
same capital numerous times, they rack up an enormous amount of debt. Without anyone noticing,
these funds have been using the Repo Market to swallow the debt Washington dumps into the market.
And it adds up. Between 2023 and September 2025, hedge
funds’ Treasury investments grew to a staggering $4 trillion. Meanwhile, the cash-futures
basis trade alone reached $830 billion. The global monetary system is being part-financed
by a tiny cabal of private funds operating with the kind of leverage that would terrify even the
most grizzled Wall Street investor. These hedge funds are banking everything on repo markets
remaining stable. As long as that happens, the game continues. DC can keep dumping its debt and
hedge funds can keep on pocketing their profits. But the second something changes – like a sudden,
unexpected spike in repo rates– the whole basis trade self-destructs. And if that happens, hedge
funds can’t ease their way out of the market. They have to evacuate ASAP.
It means liquidating their positions immediately. They have to sell off their physical bonds and buy
back their futures contracts. If dozens of funds all did that at the same time,
cashing in hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of Treasuries overnight, it would be catastrophic.
Bond prices would crash. Yields would surge. And waves of automated margin calls would be
triggered to the very same hedge funds. They’d have to sell off even more Treasuries in a
market that is increasingly running out of buyers. Foreign central banks wouldn’t want them. Neither
would pension funds. Even primary American banks wouldn’t be able to step in and save the day due
to the Basel III regulations. What happens next?
The market for US debt screeches to a frightening halt.
And it’s not impossible as it sounds. It’s happened once before. Back in 2020,
when the drama of the COVID-19 pandemic was still unfolding, the basis trade broke down.
Investors run for the exits, and automated margin calls were triggered on futures positions of the
wealthiest hedge funds all across America. To raise the money they needed to survive,
they dumped bonds. Lots of them.
The big banks couldn’t afford to buy the sudden surge of government debt. The Treasury market
suffered a brief but shocking breakdown. Credit and mortgage markets were pushed
to the brink of collapse until the Federal Reserve stepped in to contain the crisis.
Resorting to some of the most drastic economic measures in modern history, the Fed funneled
more than a trillion dollars into the system. They promised to buy up huge swathes of bonds, giving
the hedge funds the buyers they so sorely needed. A crisis had been averted.
But the foundations were already being laid for the next one.
And regulators failed to learn their lesson. They didn’t take action to bring the basis
trade under control. Instead, they effectively allowed hedge funds to
get away with even more reckless spending. And we’re seeing the consequences play out now.
As Washington’s debt spirals, the basis trade is worth more than ever
before. But the infrastructure underpinning this mechanism has migrated beyond America’s borders.
An October 2025 report from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve revealed hedge funds had
moved much of their business to offshore tax havens, like the Cayman Islands. And they can
enjoy a whole lot of benefits, like escaping corporate income tax and capital gains tax.
More importantly, the regulatory freedom allows investors to set up highly leveraged trading
vehicles without anyone asking questions. That means the engine funding America’s
debt is running completely outside the U.S. government's jurisdiction.
The next time the basis trade falls apart – which is almost inevitable – the Fed can’t step in and
put out the fire with a quick fix solution. And with every day that passes, the world
draws closer to that financial doomsday scenario. The numbers are all moving in the wrong direction.
Debt has crossed $40 trillion. Annual interest payments alone exceed $1 trillion. DC is in a
nosedive so steep that there’s almost no way to pull up and avoid a crash.
Every prospective solution creates additional problems.
The Fed can raise interest rates to calm inflation. But that just makes
maturing debt even more expensive to refinance. And with the conventional stable buyers – like
foreign central banks and pension funds – edging out of the market, Washington is becoming
reliant on short term, profit hungry hedge fund traders. And it’s the whole world that will pay.
When the trade breaks, a cascade of leveraged sell orders will automatically execute. Positions will
be liquidated immediately. Central banks will be forced to make emergency interventions as
chaos tears through borrowing costs, mortgage rates, and corporate balance sheets worldwide.
Once that financial trigger has been pulled, there is no putting the bullet back in the chamber.
